title: A Portrait for the Cellar
premise: Xanthe Galloway has spent her career as a live-in hospice nurse perfecting the art of being unnoticed, keeping meticulous counts of doors and lights because she hears the dying counting backwards toward something. When she takes a final placement at Hollowmere House caring for the reclusive Edith Vane, every mirror in the estate begins reflecting rooms one second late—and in that stolen second, Xanthe sees what was invited in generations ago by a Vane ancestor desperate to survive a winter that should have killed them all. As Edith's last night approaches and the lawyers arrive at dawn to sign the house over, the entity in the mirrors needs a living signature to renew its invitation, and it will wear the faces of everyone Xanthe has ever failed to save. Xanthe survives sunrise not by running but by refusing to sign, offering instead the one thing the house cannot counterfeit: her honest grief for the dead, which breaks the mirror-time and frees Edith to die unclaimed.
about_author: Oscar Montrose is the pen name of a former night-shift caregiver who spent six years in residential hospice work before turning to horror fiction. They write about the quiet terrors of institutional spaces and dedicate their books to the families who keep vigil.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. We meet her at a previous placement, where a dying man counts backwards from thirty and dies mid-number with his eyes fixed on the wall mirror. Xanthe's rituals—counted doors, kept lights—are established as survival tools, not quirks. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as competence; she believes invisibility keeps her safe.

chapters.title: Hollowmere Accepts Her
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She arrives at Hollowmere House to care for Edith Vane, a sharp-tongued matriarch weeks from death. The agency file is suspiciously thin; the previous three nurses all resigned without references. Edith warns her: 'Don't sign anything, don't answer anything after midnight.' Emotional beat: wary curiosity, the first flicker of found-family hope.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. On her third night, Xanthe notices the hallway mirror shows her turning her head a beat after she does. She tests it with a dropped glass—the reflection shatters late. The dying count begins again, this time from the walls themselves. Emotional beat: dread replacing routine; her rituals start failing her.

chapters.title: What Edith Won't Say
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Xanthe and Edith's 1947 diary entries. Edith's grandmother made a bargain during a famine winter—'an invitation signed in blood and ink'—to keep the family alive. Edith knows the debt comes due at her death and is terrified Xanthe will be the collateral. Emotional beat: two women circling the truth, each protecting the other badly.

chapters.title: The Faces in the Glass
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The mirrors begin showing her former patients—the ones she couldn't save—alive and forgiving her, beckoning. One offers to 'take her place' if she just signs the visitor's ledger in the front hall. Exhausted and grieving, she nearly does. Emotional beat: temptation through guilt; the price of survival made personal.

chapters.title: Doors That Weren't There
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The house grows new doors overnight; her careful count is wrong for the first time in years. She finds the sealed cellar, where a portrait of the original bargain-maker hangs over an empty frame sized for one more face—hers. Edith catches her there and finally tells her everything. Emotional beat: violation of her last defenses; truth as intimacy.

chapters.title: The Lawyers at Dawn
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Dawn brings the solicitors with inheritance papers—but the documents now include a clause no one remembers drafting, requiring 'the resident's designee' to co-sign. The entity speaks through the lead lawyer's reflection. Edith realizes the trap was never about her signature. Emotional beat: maternal fury; Edith chooses to fight rather than die quietly.

chapters.title: Nightfall Without Lights
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The power fails; every light she's counted goes dark except candleflames, which cast reflections that move independently. The dead patients walk the halls wearing borrowed faces, and the house seals itself. Xanthe and Edith barricade in the cellar beneath the portrait. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into solidarity—they hold hands like family.

chapters.title: The Last Signature
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, climax. At 3 a.m., the entity offers its final bargain: sign, and Edith lives another year; refuse, and both die tonight. Xanthe refuses—not with defiance but with honest mourning, naming aloud every patient she lost and grieving them openly. Unscripted grief is the one thing the mirrors can't reflect or counterfeit. The portrait cracks; the second-lag collapses. Emotional beat: catharsis; invisibility abandoned for witness.

chapters.title: Sunrise, Unsigned
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, resolution. Edith dies at dawn, peacefully, mid-count reaching zero on her own terms, with Xanthe holding her hand. The papers remain unsigned; the house passes to a trust that will see it demolished. Xanthe keeps one small mirror from the cellar—as a reminder, not a wound—and walks out the counted front door into full daylight. Emotional beat: grief carried openly; found family honored in loss.
